r.x: The Fugitive Slaves Pipe

is a fully carved meerschaum pipe signed F. J. Kaldenberg, depicting a woman and a man fleeing dogs. The name does not come from its own period; it was used in the catalog of an auction held in Virginia in February 2016. The pipe is today held in the collection of the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, registered under number 2016.166.37.1ab-.2. The piece is often cited both for the subject matter typical of carved meerschaum and for how the same object is described differently in two separate institutional texts.
The Object Itself

The museum record counts the pipe as New York-made and dates it to 1869-1889; the signature belongs to the workshop described in the Kaldenberg company entry. The body's material is sepiolite, the mineral name for meerschaum. The scene spreads around the chamber: the carved upper surface of the stump serves as the tobacco chamber, a woman runs past the stump looking back over her shoulder, and a man raises an axe over his head trying to fend off three dogs. With the mouthpiece, the total length is a little over nineteen centimeters. The pipe is preserved in a hinged wooden box painted black and shaped to its silhouette; the interior is lined with red velvet and satin, and the satin surface bears the maker's stamp. The museum record states plainly that the figures' faces are rendered as simian caricatures, and the institution separately notes that it collects objects carrying racist imagery in order to document the historical context in which they were produced.
The Link to the Ansdell Painting
Both the sale description and the museum record tie the scene to English painter Richard Ansdell's (1815-1885) 1861 painting
The Hunted Slaves

. The painting was shown that same year at the Royal Academy exhibition in London, accompanied by lines drawn from Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's poem about a fugitive slave taking refuge in a swamp; it is today held at the Walker Art Gallery, part of National Museums Liverpool, under number WAG 3070. The connection seems plausible at first glance, given the matching elements of the fleeing pair, the attacking dogs, and the raised axe. However, pipe literature notes that no contemporary document has been found tying the design to that source, and no period writing about the painting mentions such a pipe. Since the sources diverge on this point, the relationship is treated as an accepted attribution rather than a proven copy.
Catalog Description versus Museum Record

The pipe was, according to records, the only pipe lot in a sale of a Black American history collection assembled over many years and dispersed through Quinn's Auction Galleries in Falls Church, Virginia, and it closed, by the same records, well above the estimate range. As the accession number indicates, the piece entered the museum's collection that same year as a donation from the Liljenquist family. Set side by side, the two descriptions do not fully agree: the sale text describes the mouthpiece as amber, while the museum record gives the material as plastic; the catalog calls the box leather, while the museum describes it as wood painted black. The location of the painting also diverges in the same way: the sale text points to the International Slavery Museum in Liverpool, while National Museums Liverpool lists the work under the Walker Art Gallery in its own record; since both institutions fall under the same umbrella, this is more a difference in naming than a contradiction. Such discrepancies are exactly why an auction description should be treated as a starting point to verify rather than a final record; the subject is also discussed further in the pipe auctions entry.

r.x: Merchant Service

is a British pipe brand founded in London in the 1930s by Herbert Merchant, one that made its name in the interwar years. Rather than a wide range of shapes, the brand is remembered for a single silhouette: a small-bowled billiard with a long, pencil-thin stem. Today this proportion is linked in the community with the name of Bing Crosby; makers and factories alike have listed the same line in their own catalogs under names like "Bing" or "Bing's Favourite."
The Early London Years

Merchant Service Ltd. made its pipes in London; surviving pieces are usually stamped "MERCHANT SERVICE" and "LONDON MADE," alongside a shape number. Although the catalog included classic forms familiar from the English and French traditions, the brand's reputation was built on the slender-stemmed billiard.

Herbert Merchant died in 1944, yet production continued into the mid-century. Records indicate the firm later passed into the hands of Holland Penny Limited, with the brand rights eventually transferring to Imperial Tobacco. Sources do not give precise dates or the exact order of these two transitions.
The Birth of the "Bing" Proportion

The verifiable side of the naming is simple: Crosby was photographed time and again with pipes of this proportion, and the shape gradually came to bear his name. The rest is legend. As the story goes, the two men met on a golf course, where the singer took a liking to the pencil-thin stem on Merchant's own pipe and had similar ones made for himself; the details vary from source to source. The practical rationale for the shape is clear enough, though: with the bowl held well away from the face, smoke doesn't sting the eyes, and the stem doesn't block the line of sight.

The proportion soon made its way into other makers' shape charts as well. Peterson's 445 "Long Pastime," which appears in its 1937 catalog and stretches to seven inches, is one of the most extreme examples of this family; Savinelli, for its part, listed the shape outright under the name "Bing's Favorite." A single brand's signature thus became one of the industry-wide examples of how shape names get absorbed into common trade usage.
A Second Life in America

The English firm's trail went cold before the century was out; its name returned to circulation only in the 21st century, thanks to two Americans who took over the brand rights. Gregory Polla and Len Fogel met through their shared membership in the Hudson Valley Pipe Club. Fogel's background was on the retail side: a pipe smoker since his youth, he had worked at specialist tobacconists including the Connoisseur in New York, and once he retired from hospital administration he found time for his own pipe project. Polla, by contrast, came from a background of automotive service, machining, and woodworking — a name who knew the production side.

Polla's path into pipemaking dates to 2013. The decisive contact was meeting Bill Feuerbach, who had headed S. M. Frank & Co.; through him Polla got the chance to hear factory methods directly from a man who had overseen production for major American factory brands like Kaywoodie, Yello-Bole, and Medico. Joseph Skoda and Rolando Negoita, from the same club, also mentored him in the early days. The division of labor settled naturally: Fogel took design and concept, Polla the workbench. Records indicate the pair began working together in 2018, and the new Merchant Service was introduced in 2019.

Polla avoids the labels "handmade" or "artisan" for the pipes he turns out in batches; by his own description, this is a small one-man factory. A limited number of classic shapes are produced to repeatable dimensions, with the "Standard" billiard true to the original proportion alongside a larger-bowled "Special." His own one-off pieces bearing his personal signature form a separate line, marked "Merchant Service Originals."

r.x: Tom Dunn
was the publisher who let the pipe community find itself in the pre-internet era. In 1964 he founded both the loosely organized
The Universal Coterie of Pipe Smokers
and
The Pipe Smoker's Ephemeris

, the magazine that became the group's voice; he edited and distributed it single-handedly until his death in 2005. Records give Dunn a birth year of 1938, and he ran the publication out of his home in Queens, New York.
How the Magazine Was Made

For forty years, the Ephemeris stayed a one-man operation. Text was typed on a mechanical typewriter, pages were run off on a mimeograph machine in the early decades, and envelopes were stuffed at the house in Queens. Dunn himself described the publication as an "irregular quarterly," and indeed the interval between issues was never fixed — some years passed with only a single number. There was never a subscription fee; getting on the mailing list simply required writing in.

Most of the pages were filled with readers' letters. A correction to a brand's history, notes from a visit to a tobacconist in some faraway city, an announcement of a newly printed book, personal impressions of tobacco, and information supplied by makers and firms could all sit side by side in the same issue. The broader landscape of this kind of publication is covered in the entry on pipe books and periodicals.
The Ephemeris as an Address Book

The magazine's real influence on the community came less from the information it carried than from the contacts it created. New Coterie members' addresses were announced in every issue, and every four years these were compiled into a comprehensive collector's directory; archival records indicate eight editions of this directory were produced. In the years before email and forums, these lists were, in practice, the only way for collectors who otherwise had no idea of each other's existence to correspond by mail and phone, trade pipes, and navigate a narrow field of interest. The magazine, alongside the local clubs that proliferated in the same period, is credited with nourishing the pipe club culture.
Recognition and Archive

When the Chicagoland Pipe Collectors Club first awarded the title of Doctor of Pipes in 1998, Dunn was one of the two people honored, the other being Frank Burla. The title, awarded to two people a year, requires at least twenty years of contribution to the hobby.

The magazine closed with Dunn's death in 2005. The paper records of both the Ephemeris and the Coterie — correspondence, newspaper clippings, original artwork, collector directories, and proofs of the two volumes later turned into books — are preserved in the George Arents Tobacco Collection in the Rare Books Division of the New York Public Library. For Dunn's life story, see the entry on Thomas Allan Dunn (1938-2005).

r.x: Netsuke

is the small toggle in traditional Japanese dress that kept items hanging from the sash from falling. Since the kimono has no pockets, items such as tobacco pouches, pipe cases, seals, and medicine boxes were tied to the waist by a cord, with a toggle at the end of the cord hooked over the top edge of the wrapped sash (obi) to hold the set in place. The other links in this arrangement were the cord (himo) connecting the pieces and the single-holed bead (ojime) that cinched the cord; details are covered in the Japanese personal smoking set entry.
From Utility to Sculpture

The netsuke is accepted to have emerged in something like its familiar form in the 17th century. It spread widely through the Edo period (1603-1868); while its function stayed the same, its carved character came to the fore, and the toggle turned into a branch of miniature sculpture with standards of its own. Makers were called netsuke-shi. The field's earliest compendium is the
Sōken Kishō

, published in Osaka in 1781 by Inaba Tsūryū; the book introduces more than fifty masters, sometimes with illustrations of their work. After 1868, the spread of Western-style dress weakened the custom of hanging items from the sash, and the netsuke withdrew from everyday use.
Main Forms

Toggles are named for their shape. The most common is katabori, carved fully in the round and typically a few centimeters long. Manju is a flat, circular type named after a round confection. Kagamibuta resembles manju but has a metal lid inlaid into its center. Ryusa is carved with lattice-like openwork, while sashi has a long, rod-like shape. The range of materials is wide: ivory, boxwood and other hardwoods, horn, bone, metal, lacquer, ceramic. Newer materials such as celluloid were added to the list toward the end of the 19th century.
Smoking-Specific Types

Some of the toggles attached to smoking sets relate directly to fire. Examples cast in brass with a hollow, bowl-shaped interior are said to have been used to hold an ember for a while when lighting a kiseru. The shapes given to these bowls were drawn from everyday life: a wooden percussion instrument used to keep time in Buddhist rites (mokugyo), a shallow, wide-brimmed soldier's cap (jingasa), and more rarely a samurai helmet (kabuto). Records point to a far rarer type dating back to the 17th century: a working miniature flintlock mechanism set inside a walnut-sized metal shell, known as hiuchi-bako; this curiosity-inducing device never caught on widely. The business of fire and ash indoors was, in any case, already handled by the tabako-bon tray.

In everyday pairings, the toggle's form was chosen to suit the body of the pouch. A soft leather or cloth pouch was mostly matched with a flat manju or kagamibuta, while a hard-bodied tobacco container (tonkotsu) could be carried with any toggle type, especially katabori. Records suggest a common set arrangement in the last quarter of the 19th century ran as follows: a kagamibuta-shaped toggle in ivory or celluloid, a multi-strand silver chain hanging from it, a fixed ring-shaped ojime on the chain, and a decorated pouch at the end.
Interest Today

Netsuke is regarded today as an art form in its own right, and museums usually classify it separately from tobacco items. Even so, the pipe case (tsutsu) and the tonkotsu are considered together with netsuke because they share the same language of carving and ornament. Japanese terms mentioned in this entry are gathered in the Japanese pipe terminology glossary.

r.x: Pipe clubs

are communities of pipe and tobacco enthusiasts who meet at regular intervals, most often with a charter and a formal membership structure. Their organized form today is a product of the 20th century, but the idea itself reaches much further back, to the shared tables of English coffeehouses and the separate tobacco rooms of gentlemen's clubs. The tradition of a shared space built around the pipe has, over three centuries, moved from the corner of a coffeehouse to the club lounge, and from there to independent associations.
The Coffeehouse: Conversation for a Penny

th-century coffeehouses, which spread across England from the second half of the century onward, were unusually permeable gathering places for their time. A penny paid at the door bought the right to sit by the fire for hours, browse the newspapers, and join the conversation at the table. Tobacco was an ordinary part of this setting too. Because they offered cheap access to information, they came to be called "penny universities." Toward the end of the 18th century, as tea consumption rose and membership-only clubs gained strength, coffeehouses fell out of favor, and gentlemen's clubs largely took over their gathering function. In the "Two-penny Club," an example recorded in social-history compendia and dated to the reign of Queen Anne (1702–1714), it was a written rule that every member fill his pipe from his own tobacco box.
The Tobacco Room in Clubs

Gentlemen's clubs were born in London's West End in the 17th century; the St James's area where they clustered is still known today as "clubland." By the end of the 19th century, London had more than four hundred clubs. Yet the pipe was kept out of these lounges for a long time. Smoking was initially forbidden at the Garrick Club, founded in 1831; members reportedly either stepped outside or took refuge in a shed in the back garden. That shed was later converted into the club's tobacco room. It is recorded that for the tobacco room of the King Street building in Covent Garden, stage painters Clarkson Stanfield and David Roberts prepared large-scale canvases, and that the club moved to its current premises on Garrick Street in 1864.

th century, after its midpoint, saw the tobacco room become a standard part of club architecture. The smoking jacket, which appeared in the same years, was the garment of this arrangement: sewn from velvet, cashmere, or flannel, it absorbed smoke and kept falling ash from damaging other clothing. The garment's popularity is linked to the growing interest in Oriental tobacco in Britain during the Crimean War years. The 1867 novel
Under Two Flags
by the novelist Maria Louise Ramé, writing under the pen name Ouida, is one of the early works to portray the tobacco room as a literary refuge; the description also mentions meerschaum.
Tobacco Assemblies on the Continent

On the European continent, a similar tradition took root not in the club but around the court. The tobacco assembly (Tabakskollegium), likely originating in the Netherlands and taken up as a custom in the courts of Berlin and Potsdam in the 17th century, reached its best-known form under Prussian King Frederick William I. In rooms furnished with nothing but heavy oak tables and backless benches, and open only to men, these assemblies smoked clay pipes, drank plenty of beer, and discussed current events, religion, and politics. His son Frederick II, who disliked pipe smoke and preferred snuff, brought the tradition to an end.
From Club to Independent Association

th century, the idea of a shared space moved beyond the club building. Independent pipe clubs were founded that met regularly, introduced blends and pipes, and gave presentations on collecting and history; these gradually united under national federations. The "Pipe Smoker of the Year" award, launched in Britain in the mid-1960s and held every January in London, was the most visible product of this organizing. The award was discontinued in 2004, citing regulations restricting tobacco promotion, and was held once more in 2014 under the UK Federation of Pipe Clubs. Clubs are today recognized as playing an important role in passing on the community's accumulated knowledge and guiding newcomers.
For the meanings the pipe has acquired across the ages, see The World History of the Pipe; for well-known names in this culture, see Famous Pipe Smokers.

r.x: Türkiye's tobacco regions

form the historic homeland of Oriental tobacco, known in the world's pipe blends as "Turkish" or "Oriental." This group of small-leaved, sun-cured aromatic tobaccos has been grown since Ottoman times across a broad geography stretching from the Aegean to the Black Sea and from Thrace to southeastern Anatolia. Records indicate that the first commercial planting of tobacco on Ottoman soil took place in 1583 around Milas, in the sanjak of Menteşe, and by the end of the 16th century cultivation had spread across a wide area from Aydın and Bursa to Rumelia. Tobacco's arrival in the Ottoman Empire is a story in its own right; this entry instead covers the regions where the plant took root in these lands.
Aegean: İzmir Tobacco

Known in Western sources by its historic name, Smyrna, İzmir tobacco is the most widespread origin and is thought to account for roughly half of the world's Oriental tobacco production today. Its leaves are very small; after harvest they are strung and sun-dried. High in sugar and essential oils, and low in nicotine even by Oriental standards, it lends a blend a slightly tangy-sweet, bready-spicy character. In the 19th century, leaf exported through the port of İzmir was sought-after raw material for the Egyptian and British cigarette industries, and a significant share of the Turkish leaf used in the American-blend cigarettes that began with Camel in 1913 also originated in İzmir. In the pipe world, the "Oriental" component of English blends is usually made up largely of İzmir-heavy mixtures.
Black Sea: Samsun-Bafra

The tobaccos grown along the Black Sea coast around Samsun, and especially in the Bafra Plain, are counted among the finest examples of Oriental tobacco. Their small, oval leaves range from red to deep red, and are glossy, fine-veined, and supple; the smoke is considered full, sweet, and aromatic, with a slow, even burn. Tobacco growing has deep roots in the region going back at least to the 18th century; Bafra's tobacco heritage is preserved at the Bafra Tobacco Museum, opened in 2018 and Türkiye's first tobacco museum. In the 2000s, single-origin blends such as "Classic Samsun," from the Grand Orientals line by McClelland, reintroduced this leaf's name to pipe smokers.
The Thrace and Rumelia Heritage

Among the most celebrated origins of Ottoman-era Oriental tobacco were Rumelian towns that now lie outside Türkiye's borders: Karasu Yenicesi, known in Western sources as Yenidje (today's Genisea, in the Greek province of Xanthi — not to be confused with Yenice-i Vardar in Macedonia), İskeçe (Xanthi), and Kırcali. Yenice leaf, regarded as the most prized example of the fine-veined "basma" class, is considered to have been among the world's most expensive tobaccos in the 19th century, and it was used as a mark of quality in the advertising of classic blends, most notably Balkan Sobranie. The Balkan Wars and the population exchange that followed left these origins within Greece and Bulgaria; the name "Yenidje" nonetheless lived on within the Balkan blend tradition. On the Turkish side, cultivation continued in Thrace and the Marmara region.
Current Status

Türkiye remains today among the world's leading producers and exporters of Oriental tobacco; alongside the Aegean and the Black Sea, production also continues in southeastern and eastern Anatolia (around Adıyaman and Bitlis), largely on small family farms. Most of the crop goes into cigarette blends; the share used in pipe blends is small. Turkish pipe smokers came to know this leaf mainly through the Tekel pipe tobaccos produced for many years by the state monopoly. Tobacco expertise is also regarded as part of this heritage, standing as a deep-rooted profession unique to Türkiye.

r.x: Duke Street–stamped DRs

make up the earliest generation of Dunhill pipes. In this period, before year codes came into use, the main way to date a body was the address struck on the shank; and the DR stamp, the top-grade marker, is first seen in these same years.
The Dating Value of the Address Stamp

Alfred Dunhill's tobacco shop opened in 1907 in London's St James's district, on Duke Street. The brand is generally held to have begun making its own pipes in 1910. Products from these early years carry, alongside the word DUNHILL on the shank, the wording DUKE ST. S.W. According to the records, this wording was dropped in October 1918 and replaced with LONDON. A Duke Street stamp therefore places a pipe on its own between 1910 and late 1918, and is considered the era's most reliable dating clue. Since the brand's only smooth finish in these same years was Bruyere, every straight-grained pipe from this window also came out in that finish.
DR and Dot Marks

The DR stamp was reserved for bodies whose grain ran straight from end to end, and it marked the top rung of production. To distinguish grades within this group, small square dots were struck around the shank lettering; whether the dot fell before or after the address wording, and on which side of the DUNHILL lettering, determined the grade. According to assessments based on catalogs and collection surveys, three grades were used until roughly the mid-1920s, after which a fourth, higher grade was added. A detailed breakdown of the grades is covered in the square stamp on pre-war Bruyere DRs article.

Examples that break from this pattern have also been documented. Single Duke Street DRs carrying an oval dot instead of a square one, or with the dot struck in an unusual position, have entered the record. Whether this variation was a deliberate distinction or simply a lapse in workshop practice has not been determined; writers on the subject note that no documentary basis for either explanation exists.
The Fate of Flawed Bodies

Among early straight-grain pipes are examples with exceptional grain that nonetheless carry a hairline crack or a natural sand pit on the surface. In the years when the brand was still a small operation tied to a single shop, disposing of such a body entirely was not easy; over the following decade, a proper sorting system took shape. Dunhill first put flawed bodies on the market under separate stamps, and, according to the records, brought in the Parker brand for this purpose in the early 1920s. The Shell finish achieved through sandblasting, patented in 1917, offered a second outlet as well; but since a thin-walled chamber was not suited to sandblasting, this option was not available for every body.

r.x: Eskişehir meerschaum carving

is the craft tradition, centred in Eskişehir — the principal source of block meerschaum suitable for pipe-making — that turns this stone into pipes and figural works. A craft that works the soft stone with relief-level delicacy, it has continued since the first workshops opened in the 1920s, taken firm root in the city following a ban on raw-stone exports, and gone on to receive geographic-indication protection.
From Vienna's Workshops to Eskişehir

In the Ottoman period, meerschaum was a significant export item; the stone, however, was largely sold raw, with the carving done in workshops in Vienna and Budapest. For this reason the stone was sometimes called "Vienna stone" in Europe. In contrast to the deep-rooted history of Tophane pipe-making, which produced red-clay pipe bowls, finished-pipe production in Eskişehir only developed in the 20th century. Records indicate the city's first pipe workshop was opened in the mid-1920s by Ali Osman Denizköpüğü (1897-1961), who promoted meerschaum at domestic and international fairs and trained a great many carvers. The real turning point came in 1972, when the export of raw meerschaum was banned: with unworked stone no longer able to leave the country, carving became a stand-alone profession in Eskişehir, while block-meerschaum pipe production in Europe effectively came to an end.
The Eskişehir School and Its Masters

The signature of the Eskişehir school is figural carving: sultans' heads, mythological scenes, animal figures. Mastery here is measured not by cleanliness of form and line, as in the briar tradition, but by relief-sculpture craftsmanship; in this respect the tradition stands apart from the Western notion of the artisan pipe. İsmail Özel, nicknamed "The Artist," is regarded as one of the 20th century's greatest meerschaum carvers and the school's emblematic figure: in his Eskişehir shop in the 1970s he specialized in large figural works, is said to have carved museum-quality pieces for American collectors, and gave carving demonstrations before audiences. Today the number of active masters in the city is put at around sixty; İsmail Bağlan, Said Altınay, and Muhsin Erdoğan are counted among the well-known names of the contemporary generation.
From the Well to the Beeswax: The Craft Process

The stone is extracted, in nodule form, from well and gallery mining meters underground in villages such as Beyazaltın (formerly Sepetçi), Sarısu, and Söğütçük. Since it carves easily while still damp from the well, carvers prefer to work it before it dries out. Traditional production passes through stages known as rough-cutting, roughing, finishing, and heat-treating; the finished pipe is then dipped in a beeswax bath to be polished. This waxing is what makes possible the stone's most beloved trait: as it is smoked, the pipe "colours" as it absorbs tar, moving from white to golden-yellow and on to amber and reddish-brown tones — a colouring process regarded among collectors as an important measure of value.
Geographic Indication and Museum

"Eskişehir Meerschaum" is protected as a designation of origin under registration no. 26 with the Turkish Patent and Trademark Office, and is counted among Turkey's first geographic indications in the mining sector. The craft's memory is kept alive in Odunpazarı: the Meerschaum Museum, opened in 2008 within the Kurşunlu Complex, is the world's first museum dedicated to meerschaum and holds around 400 works by roughly 60 artists. The Odunpazarı Municipality has also been running a festival since 2018 to introduce the craft to new generations.

r.x: The pipe in art and literature

has been painted and written about for four centuries not merely as an object but as a carrier of meaning. In the painter's or the writer's hand, the pipe is at times a reminder of life's brevity, at times the standard prop of the thinking man, and at times the single stroke that defines a character.
In Painting: A Warning Made of Smoke

After tobacco spread across Europe, pipe-smoking figures multiplied rapidly in 17th-century Dutch and Flemish painting. Adriaen Brouwer and Adriaen van Ostade, who trained in the circle of Frans Hals, are counted among the artists who placed ordinary pipe-smokers in tavern and village scenes at the center of the canvas. Many of these paintings do more than record daily life; by the moral standards of the time they also carry a warning against excessive pleasure. Smoke that quickly disperses is read, in the vanitas tradition, as the visual counterpart of life's transience.

th century, the emphasis shifted. Vincent van Gogh's self-portrait, painted in Arles in January 1889, showing him with a bandaged ear and a pipe, suggests that the pipe had become a mark of an inward state rather than a moral lesson. Of the two bandaged self-portraits he made in the weeks after injuring his ear, the one with the pipe is in a private collection and is only rarely exhibited; the other version of the bandaged self-portrait is at the Courtauld Gallery in London. Paul Cézanne's
The Card Players

series, worked on between 1890 and 1895, builds the same quiet attentiveness. In the first two of the five finished canvases, a man with a pipe stands beside the players; the study he made for this figure,
Man with a Pipe
, is associated with the series.
The best-known painting on the subject, though, is René Magritte's 1929 work
La trahison des images

. Beneath a meticulously rendered pipe are the words "Ceci n'est pas une pipe" ("This is not a pipe"), because the object on the canvas cannot be smoked — it is only a representation. Held in the collection of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the work has become one of the most cited images in modern art for the way it interrogates the relationship between word and image.
In Literature: An Extension of Character

In literature the pipe is often used as a device that measures the length of thought. In Arthur Conan Doyle's 1891 story "The Red-Headed League," Sherlock Holmes describes a puzzle as "a three pipe problem" and asks not to be disturbed for fifty minutes. Sidney Paget, who illustrated the first editions of the stories, drew Holmes with a straight pipe; the curved calabash shape that comes to mind today actually comes from the stage rather than the text. This shape is generally attributed to the American actor William Gillette, who played the character hundreds of times; according to the story, a curved pipe was preferred because it could be held between the teeth while delivering lines and gesturing, making both easier. Since no period photograph or direct testimony confirms that Gillette actually used a calabash on stage, the connection cannot be taken as certain. The staying power of this visual template can also be traced in later collections such as the Peterson Sherlock Holmes series.

The same function persists in other narratives: in J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth, the pipe is a detail that conveys a people's temperament and everyday rhythm; the scope of this detail is covered in the entry Pipes and Pipe-weed in The Lord of the Rings. For the particular place meerschaum has held in poetry and prose, see Meerschaum in Literature. The public image real people have built around the pipe is gathered under famous pipe smokers.

r.x: A Conversation With Damiano Rovera

is the title of a written interview conducted with Damiano Rovera, fourth-generation maker at the Italian pipe brand Ardor. The questions were prepared by Bear Graves, the answers were gathered not in person but by email, and the text was published by Smokingpipes.com; it entered the pipe community's archives in 2007. It is cited as one of a limited number of records to document, in the maker's own words, how an Italian family workshop operates.
Nature of the Document

The text is not the transcript of a single sitting but consists of written answers to questions posed in sequence; for that reason the subject headings are sharply separated from one another. At the time the answers were given, Damiano was producing alongside his father, Dorelio Rovera. Concrete facts that can be drawn from the document include that the workshop is closed to visitors, that a separate showroom is operated instead, and that the brand's distribution in the United States was handled by Steve Monjure.
The Rovera Family and Ardor

The family's briar business begins with the Società Rovera, founded in Varese in 1911; the workshop was founded by four Rovera brothers, and in the early years the lathes were run on water power. The second generation's name is Angelo Rovera, and the third is his son Dorelio, who began working briar in 1958. The name Ardor derives from these two names: Angelo Rovera's initials (AR) combined with the first syllable of Dorelio's name (DOR). The brand was founded in 1974, with production continuing in Gavirate, in the province of Varese.

Damiano is the family's fourth generation; together with his brother Dimitri, he now runs the business. Sources give differing figures for annual output, but in every case it stays at a scale a handful of hands could produce at a bench. This in-between position makes the brand one of the examples showing that the line between artisan pipe and factory pipe cannot be drawn with a hard edge. Blocks are gathered from Sardinia, Liguria, Calabria, and Tuscany; records state they are air-dried for roughly ten years before being worked. Mouthpieces are cut in the workshop from acrylic sheet; the flared, flattened "pennellessa" shape is considered the brand's signature, while some series use a silver-banded (spigot) joint instead. Series names are drawn largely from celestial bodies: Urano, Marte, Mercurio, Giove, Venere, Nettuno, Plutone, and Meteora are among the main ones.
Topics Covered in the Interview

The questions range widely, from the workshop's daily routine to the brand's market geography. Topics on record include the design approach, the mark left by Danish pipemaking, Rovera's own eponymous series, the buyer geography for the large-volume Giant models, and the maker's own tobacco preference.

The eponymous series, while coming from the same workshop as Ardor, is defined as a separate signature; while Ardor continues as the joint work of two generations, this line reflects a single maker's own preferences. The main influence cited in the interview is the Danish school: staining that uses contrasting tones together to bring out the grain is, according to this series, its distinguishing trait in terms of finish. It is also from this same text that we know almost all buyers of the Giant series are in the United States. On the tobacco side, Rovera states his preference runs toward English-style blends.

r.x: Britain

is one of the select countries that shaped pipemaking in both its clay and its briar phases. The clay pipe workshops founded after tobacco reached the island supplied the European market for centuries, and the briar workshops that gathered around London in the second half of the 19th century gave rise to a distinct approach to shape and craftsmanship known as the "English pipe."
The Clay Pipe Centuries

The product of the first phase was the clay pipe. Shaped in a mold and fired, these cheap pipes remained, until the spread of cheap cigarettes at the end of the 19th century, almost the sole smoking implement in Europe. Production was organized early on: in 1619 the pipemakers of Westminster were formed into a body by royal charter, and within a few decades this structure was folded into London's livery-company system. Outside London, the town of Broseley in Shropshire became the best-known provincial center, with production reportedly beginning at the end of the 16th century; the practice of date-stamping pipes by makers there in the last quarter of the 17th century remains one of the anchors of archaeological dating today. The town's last clay pipe factory ceased production at the end of the 1950s, and the building reopened as a museum in 1996.
The Arrival of Briar and the London Workshops

After the 1850s, briar of Corsican origin reached the island via France and quickly pushed clay into the background. For the background to this shift, see The Briar Revolution and Saint-Claude. The step that set the direction of the trade in Britain was Henri Comoy, of the Saint-Claude-based Comoy family, settling in London in 1879 and opening a small workshop in Seven Dials (today's Cambridge Circus area); Comoy's of London is thus considered the pioneer of briar production in the country. Silversmith Benjamin Barling's Barling, founded in 1812 and known for fitting silver bands and caps to meerschaum pipes, continued for a long time to finish briar bowls turned in France under its own brand; it began working its own bowls in England around 1906. In these same years, Alfred Dunhill, who came from the leather-goods and motoring-accessories trade, began selling pipes under his own name at his Duke Street shop in 1907.
Mergers and the Decline of the Industry

The 20th century was a period of consolidation in which scattered workshops were brought under single roofs. The Oppenheimer group acquired BBB (A. Frankau) in 1920, and within the same decade also bought Loewe & Co. and a significant share of Comoy's. This string of acquisitions led to the founding, in the 1930s, of Cadogan Investments Ltd., a holding company named after its Cadogan Square address in London. Names such as GBD, Civic, Dr. Plumb, and Sina came under the same umbrella over time. With Orlik's acquisition in 1980, the group consolidated production in a single factory purpose-built for pipemaking near Southend-on-Sea.

The market's contraction with the rise of the cigarette led many storied names to close or change hands after the war. Even so, the country's production tradition was not entirely cut off: alongside corporate manufacturers such as Dunhill (White Spot), a limited number of independent workshops continue to carry on English craftsmanship.

r.x: Novák

is the name given to the pipes produced by Czech pipe maker Michal Novák in his workshop in Prague. Born, according to records, in 1954, Novák is not a craftsman who took up the bench as a child; he moved into pipe making after a long career in writing and photography. This late start has shaped both the scale and the working method of the workshop, keeping output limited to a small number of individually designed pieces each year.
From the Writing Desk to the Bench

Novák's first profession was journalism and photography. In the 1990s his interest turned toward pipe and tobacco publishing; he is said to have taken on the role of editor at a magazine published in this field. That role took him to pipe factories and workshops in Germany, Italy, and Denmark. The knowledge he built up over years of watching and writing about other people's work went on to form the basis of his own production. According to records, he has been a member of the Académie Internationale de la Pipe, which treats the pipe as a subject of research, since 1999.

His turn toward pipe making was shaped as much by a pipe he acquired from an acquaintance in Italy as by the relationship he built with his fellow Czech maker Jan Klouček. Novák worked in Klouček's workshop and has counted himself among the makers that workshop trained. The date of his move to independent production is inconsistent across sources; the general figure given is the late 2000s. Novák is counted among the generation of Czech makers who gained visibility in those same years.
Shape and Craftsmanship

What identifies a Novák pipe at first glance is the faceted surface of the bowl. The maker tends to break up a classic, round-lined bowl with straight cuts, sharp lines, and curved planes. The geometry these edges create makes it immediately clear that a piece worked individually in this way, in the spirit of freehand design, did not come out of a mold.

The second distinguishing point is the finish. Although the workshop occasionally turns out lightly or darkly stained pieces, the bulk of production is unstained briar, simply polished. Without stain, the grain reads as it is; as the wood is used, it settles into its own colour. Novák is known for this preference, and the colour of his pipes is largely left to the root's own tone.

Vulcanite and acrylic, both common mouthpiece materials, are used for the stems. In keeping with the practice established in Central Europe, some pieces are drilled to take a 9-millimetre filter; using an adapter for those who prefer to smoke without a filter is considered normal in the region.

Keeping output low is a deliberate choice. The time given to designing each piece directly limits how many pipes the workshop can turn out in a year. In this respect, Novák is regarded as a typical example of the ring of one-person workshops that grew stronger alongside the Czech Republic's established factory tradition after the 2000s.

r.x: Grace's Guide

, fully Grace's Guide to British Industrial History, is an online reference that compiles Britain's industrial and manufacturing past through company, product, and personal records. The organization states it began publishing in 2007 and is registered as a charity in England and Wales under number 1154342. The name says nothing to a pipe enthusiast at first glance, yet tobacco and pipe manufacturing are also part of British industrial history and have found a place in the archive.
The Archive's Structure

The site works on a wiki logic. A separate page opens for each company or person, information is mostly given as bullet points arranged in chronological order, and beneath each line is noted which journal or directory it was drawn from. Most of the material comes from digitized engineering and industrial periodicals; the organization states it has scanned thousands of publications from between 1833 and 1950. The collection is not static: while around 150,000 pages and 235,000 images were reported in 2022, by early 2026 these figures had, according to the records, risen past 171,000 pages and 248,000 images; the numbers should be taken as approximate since they change as new donations are scanned. Pages can be read online for free, while downloading documents as PDF is a paid service.
What Is Found on the Tobacco and Pipe Side

The archive has a category devoted to tobacco products, and familiar names appear within it. Around Dunhill there are interlinked pages ranging from Alfred Dunhill himself to family members and the company's separate product lines. For the Liverpool tobacco manufacturer Cope Bros & Company, the archive's record shows a company registration dated 17 August 1885. Firms engaged in clay pipe manufacturing, factories, and the tobacco trade can likewise be searched.

The value of these records lies not in narrative but in dry data: founding year, incorporation date, address change, merger, change of ownership, liquidation. Verifying which legal entity a brand operated under and in which year, when read alongside patent and registration records, can settle dating disputes.
The Limits of Its Scope

The archive is British-focused from start to finish; French, German, Italian, or Turkish workshops fall outside its scope. Because the content depends on donated publications scanned by volunteers, subject coverage is also uneven; engineering and heavy industry branches predominate while tobacco is treated relatively sparsely. In the search box the English word "pipe" alone does not do the job, since results get mixed with industrial pipe manufacturers; adding tobacco, pipe, or the company name directly to the query narrows results markedly.

Like other archives in the field, Grace's Guide does not by itself illuminate the full history of a British pipe or tobacco firm. Even so, being free, open to everyone, and citing the source of every line makes it a useful first link in the verification chain.

r.x: A hypothetical World War II pipe

is the name given to a dating puzzle raised by John C. Loring, who compiled Dunhill stamps. The puzzle is set up like this: if a pipe carries on its shank only a die used exclusively during the war years, yet at the same time carries a year code that never appears with that die, what does the code date? Loring does not say he has such an example in hand; after laying out the wartime conditions, he suggests that a piece like this could turn up, and that if it did, the code would document not the manufacture but a later repair.
The Uncoded War Stamp

At Dunhill, a stamp is struck not with individual letter punches but with dies cast together as whole words and numbers. This method turns each year's code into a separate job: the dies for the following year's code have to be ordered in advance. The war broke this ordering chain, and starting in 1941 a great many Shells were stamped with a single die carrying no year code at all: "DUNHILL SHELL MADE IN ENGLAND" above, "PATENT No 1341418/20" below. Sources give the year this die fell out of use as anywhere between 1943 and 1945.

Here the absence of a code is not a gap in knowledge but knowledge itself. Because the die belongs only to these few years, the stamp's mere presence places the pipe in the war years on its own; examples that have entered repair-shop records are also assessed within this range. Records suggest a similar reading may apply to certain smooth-finish pipes that carry neither a year code nor the word "INNERTUBE." On the other hand, not every war year passed without a code; Shells dated to 1944, carrying both a year code and a different patent number, are known. The whole family of stamps is the subject of the Dunhill dating guide.
A Ten-Year Gap in the Dunhill Timeline

Behind such a necessity lies a decade in which the brand nearly stopped altogether. In April 1941, during the Blitz bombing, Dunhill's London shop was hit; it is recounted that a significant part of the firm's old records were also lost at that time. This is one of the reasons Dunhill dating relies on the stamp rather than on documents. Distribution of raw materials was put under rationing, and the restrictions did not end with the war but continued into the early 1950s. Because the brand did not put out a regular annual catalogue between 1940 and 1950, the Dunhill chronology jumps almost in a single step from the late 1930s to the early 1950s.

The clearest trace of the restriction shows up in the wood. The Italian briar sought for smooth-finish pipes became unobtainable throughout the war; the Algerian briar the Shell line relied on faced a somewhat less severe shortage. Dunhill's output of the period is both small in number and narrow in range.
A Second Reading of the Year Code

The restrictions also reached mouthpiece material: ebonite (vulcanite) was either rationed or banned outright, so horn mouthpieces are frequently found on pipes of the period. Horn's known weakness is a tendency to crack; its lifespan does not match that of the shank it is mounted on. A pipe carrying a war stamp that today wears an ebonite mouthpiece is, for this reason, expected to have had that mouthpiece replaced later. Independent repair records, however, don't leave the picture entirely one color; some war-stamped pipes are also documented with ebonite mouthpieces.

Loring's inference comes in at this point. A year code that has landed next to an uncoded war die, in his view, marks not the year the bowl was carved but the year it came back to the workshop; the code is a date of maintenance, not of manufacture. The same reading is applied to pipes made before 1922, when the year-code system began, and later repaired: there too, a lone digit gives not the age of the shank but the age of the repair. For a comparison of horn, ebonite, and other options, see the entry on mouthpiece materials.

r.x: Brigham pipes

are the products of a Canadian brand that grew out of the shop Roy Brigham opened in Toronto in 1906, and among collectors they are best known for the brass dots (dots) set into the mouthpiece. The brand never stamped a production year on its pipes in any period; the age of a Brigham is therefore estimated by reading three marks together: the text of the shank stamp, the three-digit shape number, and the count and arrangement of the mouthpiece dots. This trio is usually enough to place most examples within a decade; narrowing it down to a single year is rarely possible.
The Shank Stamp

The workshop's first-generation pipes were unfiltered, and the stamping scheme of this early period is unknown. The innovation that made the brand distinctive arrived in 1938: a filter system built around a rock-maple rod set inside the shank. Smoke passed over the porous rod, which trapped some of the moisture and tar. The system was patented in Canada and stamped on the shank as CAN PAT 372982. Seen together with a fine script logo and the three-digit shape number, this stamp is considered the most reliable marker of production from 1938 to 1955.

When the patent expired in 1955, the stamp gave way to a MADE IN CANADA line in block letters. Records suggest the logo was refreshed around 1970, with Brigham and Made in Canada set on separate lines beneath the shape number; records likewise suggest that in the early 1980s the second line was shortened to Canada, and by the end of the decade nothing was stamped beyond the shape number and logo. It's normal to see both forms overlap during a transition from one stamp style to another; the stamp alone doesn't give a narrow date.
What the Number and the Dots Say

The three-digit shape number carries two pieces of information at once: the first digit gives the pipe's quality grade, meaning how many dots are on the mouthpiece, and the following two digits give the shape. Read this way, a pipe numbered 423 belongs to the four-dot grade, shape number 23.

From 1938 to 1980, the dots were arranged according to an eight-grade system. A known complication in this system was that three dots were used in two different arrangements: on some pipes the dots ran vertically, on others horizontally, yet both variants carried 600-series shape numbers. Period catalogues list these two arrangements as separate, lower grades apart from the six-dot 600 series; sharing a shape number does not make them equivalent. The system was simplified in 1980, the vertical-horizontal three-dot distinction was dropped, and a seven-dot grade was added at the top. This seven-grade system, reports say, lasted until 2001.
Norseman, Valhalla, and President

The large, freehand bodies that spread under Danish influence in the late 1960s gave rise to two Brigham series. The fully rusticated Norseman carries a horizontal three-dot arrangement with a larger dot in the middle; a single source states its stamp began with 9W, with the trailing number (2-7) giving the shape. The smooth or partly rusticated Valhalla, meanwhile, was offered in grades A, B, and C, with C the highest; the same single source reports it carried an AV6, BV6, or CV6 stamp depending on grade for the sixth shape, with the dot count also rising from four to six. The two series merged in 1980 under the name President, distinguished by a three-dot arrangement with a larger dot on the right.
From Toronto to Europe

In 2001 production moved from Toronto to Europe; the range of shapes narrowed noticeably, and the aluminum tenon gave way to a composite part. During this period the lower lines kept their brass dots, while the upper lines lost the dots and were marked instead with a metal band bearing a leaf logo. In the seven-grade line introduced in 2007, the distinction is no longer built on dots or shape variety; grades are instead separated by names referencing Canadian history and by finishes assigned to each. The brand's never having used a year-coded stamp of the kind seen with Dunhill, and the company's not having recorded stamp changes internally, leaves dating at the level of estimation; the dot and the stamp only make sense when read together.

r.x: Airflow

refers to the cross-section of the smoke channel running from the base of the chamber to the tip of the mouthpiece in a pipe, and to how that cross-section affects the smoke. The term is also the name of a debate that has run through the community since the late 1990s: how wide should the channel be, and should the user later alter this measurement? The subject is considered the detail of pipe anatomy most directly tied to the smoking experience.
The Geometry of the Channel

Smoke enters the shank through the hole at the base of the chamber, passes the mortise-tenon junction where the shank meets the mouthpiece, travels through the channel inside the mouthpiece, and exits through the slot at the bit end. Along this path, any narrowing of the cross-section or any sharp corner disrupts the flow. The measurement has not stayed constant through history: in clay pipe records the shank-hole diameter is about 3.6 millimeters at the end of the 16th and start of the 17th century, dropping to 1.6 millimeters by the end of the 18th century. Archaeologists use this narrowing as a criterion for dating clay pipes.
The Origin of the Debate

According to the record, two articles brought the subject onto the agenda of the American pipe press. The first appeared in the winter 1996/97 issue of Pipes & Tobaccos, written by Dayton H. Matlick, on the Danish maker Lars Ivarsson. The method attributed to Ivarsson is boring a single, uniform 4-millimeter (about 5/32 inch) channel from chamber to bit end in every pipe he made. The testing method tied to this needs no tool: if a whistle is heard when drawing an ordinary breath through an empty pipe, the channel is narrow; a muffled hum or silence is taken to mean the flow is unobstructed. The stated rationale is that turbulence arising in narrow passages, where speed increases, separates moisture from the smoke onto the channel wall and makes the smoke wet.

The second article appeared in the fall 1997 issue of the same magazine, written by Rick Newcombe; this time the subject was widening the channel of a pipe one already owned after the fact. Newcombe's views on the topic later also appeared in his book
In Search of Pipe Dreams

, published by Sumner Books. Newcombe relates that Jim Benjamin, who taught him the practice, had been widening the channels of his own pipes since the late 1940s. It is said the pair's measurements initially ranged between 5/32 and 11/64 inch, later rising to as much as 3/16 inch (about 4.8 millimeters) depending on the length and shape of the pipe, with 5/32 inch regarded as the lower limit.
Objections

Several arguments are voiced on the opposing side. The most concrete is the view that a wide channel overheats the chamber and over time leads to burnout; makers holding this view cite their own workbench experience rather than measurement as support. The second reflects a collector's perspective: a pipe one might later consider modifying should not have been bought in the first place, since any intervention alters the object's original state. The third objection concerns not the channel itself but the durability of the mouthpiece. It is said that Lars Ivarsson and Jess Chonowitsch, from the Danish school, smoked their own pipes with an open channel but did not follow the same practice on the pipes they sold; the reason given is the risk that a thinned mouthpiece could be bitten through by an inexperienced user's teeth.
Limits of the Practice

Widening the channel is irreversible: once enlarged, a hole cannot be narrowed again. The difficulty lies not in the shank but in the mouthpiece; for the cross-section to stay even all the way to the bit end, the inside of the vulcanite — rubber hardened with sulfur — is filed out. Since it is a lengthy, irreversible operation, it can end up ruining the pipe in the hands of someone unfamiliar with mouthpiece work. Vulcanite's surface dulling under the effect of light, heat, and moisture is a separate maintenance matter and should not be confused with airflow.

Channel diameter is not the only factor determining flow. Tar accumulating over time narrows the cross-section; this is why pipe cleaning is also cited in connection with sustained airflow. Overpacking the chamber, insufficiently dried tobacco, and a clogged filter produce a similar result. The common view in the community is that a hard-drawing pipe forces the smoker to pull harder, which makes tongue bite more likely. Still, since the topic is debated more through user experience than measured data, no firm consensus can be said to exist.

r.x: Portraits carved onto pipes

describes a broad production tradition in which the tobacco pipe served not only as a smoking instrument but also as a commemorative object. Throughout the nineteenth century, masters working in clay, meerschaum, wood, and porcelain carried the faces of politicians, soldiers, rulers, writers, and composers onto the bowl; figures drawn from mythology and folk tales received the same attention. For living or recently deceased subjects, the carver typically worked from a medallion, an engraving, or a photograph. For legendary figures whose faces were never known, the standard was not likeness but recognisability: a crown, a helmet, or a bunch of grapes was enough to signal who was being depicted.
Campaign and Commemorative Portraits in Clay Pipes

The clay pipe was cheap, could be reproduced by mould, and was easily replaced when broken — which is why the largest body of portrait experiments appears in this material. In the literature, such bowls are called "figural pipes" or "face pipes"; by the 19th century they had multiplied enough to form a category of their own in the cheap-souvenir market. Gambier, one of several clay pipe makers active in the French town of Givet in the mid-century, is the best-known name in the field; records show that among its more than one hundred head moulds were figures such as Queen Victoria, Napoléon, Rembrandt, Victor Hugo, and Niccolò Paganini. In the United States, meanwhile, clay pipes distributed during presidential campaigns are treated as a distinct category in the archaeological literature: examples bearing a likeness to William Henry Harrison, Millard Fillmore, Franklin Pierce, James Buchanan, and Abraham Lincoln have been recorded. According to the same literature, one such pipe was excavated in 1994 at the Poplar Forest dig in Virginia.
Carved Portraits in Meerschaum, Wood, and Porcelain

Meerschaum, because it holds fine detail so well, became the principal material for portrait carving; for the period's carving repertoire, see the entry on 19th-century carved meerschaum pipes. The most frequently cited series is the meerschaum bust set produced by New York's William Demuth firm, depicting U.S. presidents in sequence on the bowl; the idea is said to have originated from two pipes presented to President James A. Garfield in 1881. Gustav Fischer Sr., working in Boston, is also said to have carved subjects such as Mephistopheles, Buffalo Bill, and Jeanne d'Arc, as well as Directum, a famous racehorse of the era. On porcelain bowls, portraits were generally not carved but applied to the surface as a decal. Portrait carving in wood continues today: in France, Roger Vincent is said to have carved briar busts of Jules Verne, Mozart, Shakespeare, and Victor Hugo, while Ukrainian carver Max Bogdan has, since 2018, depicted contemporary film and political figures; both are considered part of the same tradition's present-day continuation. For a list of people identified with the pipe, see the entry on Famous Pipe Smokers.
Reineke Fuchs: The Cunning Fox's Career in Pipes

Animal heads were also frequently carved in pipe and cigar-holder carving, and among them the largest body of work centred on the fox. One reason for this is that the fox here was not merely an animal but a literary figure with a name and a story. The subject's roots trace back to the
Roman de Renart

, whose earliest branches are attributed to Pierre de Saint-Cloud around 1174. William Caxton brought the story into English in 1481; in 1498 the Lübeck printer Hans van Ghetelen published the Low German
Reynke de vos
, illustrated with 89 woodcut engravings. Johann Christoph Gottsched published a prose adaptation in 1752; drawing on that text, Goethe wrote the twelve-canto verse epic
Reineke Fuchs

in 1793, published in 1794. The real source for carvers, however, was the illustrated edition printed in Stuttgart in 1846: the thirty-six large plates and numerous vignettes that Wilhelm von Kaulbach (1805–1874) prepared for this volume formed a visual repertoire that meerschaum and wood carvers drew on for decades. In this way, the fox became a self-contained pipe subject, anchored in the visual language of a single book and repeated for decades afterward.

r.x: Harem Pipe

is a tabletop smoking apparatus patented in the mid-1930s and brought to market in the United States in the mid-20th century. It is not a pipe in the classical sense. It is built from three parts: a holder into which a cigarette or cigar is set at an angle, a metal ashtray base to which the holder is attached, and a flexible, braid-covered hose running from the base with a plastic mouthpiece at its end. The smoker watches the tobacco burn from a distance and draws smoke only through the end of the hose. The stamp on the underside of the base reads, alongside the product name, the slogan "The Smokers Robot," the patent number, the trio "COMFORT — LUXURY — SAFETY," and the phrase "Jonathan Law, New Haven, Conn."
The Patent Behind the Design

The number on the stamp refers to US Patent No. 2,093,760, titled "Cigarette and Cigar Holder." According to the document, the application was filed on 20 June 1935 in the name of James P. Kiernan, resident of Derby, Connecticut, and the patent was registered on 21 September 1937. The purpose section of the text comes down to three points: keeping the smoker away from the burning tobacco, preventing smoke from reaching the face and eyes, and eliminating the fire risk of smoking in bed by placing the apparatus on a side table or nightstand.

Mechanical details are also described in the document. The holder tilts toward the base's vertical axis, so that once accumulated ash reaches sufficient weight it breaks off on its own and falls into the base. When the holder's outer tube is pressed back to compress the spring inside it, the stationary inner tube holds the cigarette butt in place; the outer tube slides off over the butt, which then likewise falls into the base. The interior of the hose is lined with rubber, its exterior covered with silk or a similar weave. The patent further notes that the holder can be replaced with a bowl for smoking pipe tobacco, and that several holders can be attached to a single base so that several people around a bridge table can share the same apparatus.
Name, Form, and Association

The name "Harem" has no connection to the design's origin; it is an example of the orientalist marketing language commonly seen in American consumer goods of the period. The arrangement of a separate body connected to a braided hose visually recalls the hookah, yet the Harem Pipe has neither water nor a cooling chamber; the hose merely creates distance. The idea of keeping away from burning tobacco is not new in itself: in the Ottoman chibouk culture, the long-stemmed chibouk achieved the same distance for centuries by another means. What sets the Harem Pipe apart is that it achieves this distance through a bendable hose, and that its bowl stays fixed on the table rather than being carried in hand. The mouthpiece being plastic also reflects the mass-production trend of the era; in these years cheap synthetics were increasingly replacing classic mouthpiece materials.
A Later Version and Collecting

There is no definitive document regarding the years of production; collector records estimate the apparatus was on the market sometime between the 1940s and the 1950s. According to the same records, later versions dropped the name "Harem" and the product was stamped only with the name Jonathan Law; no independent trade record has been found for a firm of that name in New Haven. The Harem Pipe today is remembered less as part of the mainstream of pipe history than among the equipment and apparatus experiments that appear throughout the world history of the pipe; in tobacciana collecting it is likewise grouped under the heading of these curious devices.

r.x: Thomas Allan Dunn
(1938-2005) was the American publisher and compiler behind
The Pipe Smoker's Ephemeris

, widely considered the longest-running periodical in the pipe world, which he produced single-handedly for forty-one years. Known to his correspondents by his initials, "TAD," Dunn ran both the magazine and the reader community that formed around it from his home in College Point, in the New York City borough of Queens.
Life Beyond Publishing

He was the fourth of Alice and Lawrence Dunn's eight children; the College Point house where he grew up with his siblings remained his address for the rest of his life. His schooling stayed in the same neighborhood: the local St. Fidelis school, followed by Flushing High School. In 1957 he enlisted in the U.S. Army Reserve, trained at the engineer school at Fort Belvoir, Virginia, and reached the rank of Specialist 5 (sergeant) by the time of his discharge in 1964. He earned his bachelor's degree in 1969 from New York University's Washington Square College of Arts and Science. Professionally he followed his father into insurance, spending his career at Metropolitan Life in Manhattan, earning the Life Management Institute's fellow designation in 1977, and rising to a managerial post in the company's human resources division. He took early retirement in 1991 to care for his ailing parents.
The Universal Coterie Of Pipe Smokers

The Universal Coterie of Pipe Smokers (TUCOPS), which Dunn founded in 1964, can be translated as "the universal fellowship of pipe smokers." Membership was free: no dues were asked of members, no obligations expected, and the group kept no meeting calendar. New members were mailed a lapel pin and a wallet-sized membership card. By some accounts, membership peaked at around three thousand. The group's presence lived in mailboxes rather than meeting halls, which set TUCOPS apart from the face-to-face tradition of pipe clubs.
Forty-One Years Of The Ephemeris

The magazine was the group's only channel of communication. The first issue is dated December 19, 1964: a single typewritten sheet, filled front and back. Dunn described the publication's schedule as "irregularly quarterly." Over time it grew to magazine size, and some issues ran past a hundred pages. Its content shifted from newsletter to compiled archive: reader letters from around the world, poems, short stories, drawings, literary excerpts, club news, auction results, book bibliographies, Sherlock Holmes miscellany (Sherlockiana), and a "Broken Pipes" section commemorating members who had died. Dunn also catalogued members by their collecting interests, publishing the results from 1981 onward as the
Collectors Directory
; the eighth and final edition appeared in June 2004.
The magazine arrived at a moment when the field had gone quiet: by 1964, America's pipe-focused periodicals had run their course;
Pipe Lovers
(January 1946 – April 1950),
The American Smoker
, and
Pipe Smokers Review

had all folded, and nothing had replaced them. Every stage of production fell to one person. Dunn sorted incoming material by subject, handled typesetting and layout himself, and personally drove the print-ready copy to a printer in Pittsfield, Massachusetts — a round trip of more than six hundred kilometers. Distribution was his responsibility too: address labels handwritten, envelopes sorted by zip code, and sacks of mail hauled to the post office. The final issue is dated Winter-Spring 2005.
Honors And The Archive He Left Behind

Though Dunn's name was widely known in the community, he himself avoided ceremonies and gatherings. Records show that in 1988 the International Academy of the Pipe, founded in Paris in 1985, elected him its first American corresponding member; Dunn made clear from the outset that he would not attend the annual meetings. In 1998 he became one of the first two recipients of the Chicagoland Pipe Collectors Club's lifetime achievement title, "Doctor of Pipes" (the other was Frank Burla), but he was absent from that ceremony as well.

Dunn died in New York at the end of 2005, after an illness of nearly a year. His will directed that the library, correspondence, and tobacco-related documents he had gathered over the years go to an institution that would keep them open to researchers. The collection is now held by the New York Public Library's Rare Books Division in two separate holdings: an eight-box collection of magazines spanning spring 1965 to 2005, and a forty-one-box collection of correspondence covering mainly 1961 to 2005. Through it, the twentieth-century arc of pipe collecting can now be traced through a firsthand research source.

r.x: Pipe making in Sweden

is a tradition that has stayed in the shadow of neighboring Denmark, small in number but technically highly ambitious. The country's factory era was short-lived; it was really the reputation earned by a handful of solo craftsmen at the end of the twentieth century that made the name known.
The Factory Era

Sweden's first briar pipe factory was founded in 1931 in Lerum, near Gothenburg. The firm, known by the short name Svenska Rökpipfabriken (SRF), was in the hands of the Eliason family; some records credit the founding to father and son Hjalmar and Gösta Eliason together, others to Gösta alone. Gösta, who ran production, had learned the craft during a year's apprenticeship at a factory in Switzerland; according to records he was only nineteen when he took charge of the operation. The factory sourced its briar burl first from Algeria and Corsica, and in later years largely from Spain. When briar supplies became difficult during the Second World War, pear wood was used instead. Production ended in 1979 when Gösta retired; some records state the company changed hands that year and stayed in operation for a few more years.

The country's largest pipe facility was Skandinaviska Pipfabriken (SKAPI), founded in Uddevalla in 1936. Max D. Schwab came from a family that had made pipes in Cologne for two generations; after leaving 1930s Germany and settling in Sweden, he started production in a modest basement workshop that grew quickly, with the new factory building completed in 1946. The plant ceased operating in the late 1960s. Reliable information is scarce on Skånska Pipfabriken, associated with Hyllstofta in the Skåne region; it appears to have been founded before the war and never to have resumed production afterward.
The Workshop Generation

As the factories closed, Sweden's international reputation as a pipe-making nation came to rest mainly on individual craftsmen. The best known name of this generation is Bo Nordh, born in 1941 and passed away in 2006. Confined to a wheelchair after a motorcycle accident in his youth, Nordh began carving pipes from ready-drilled blanks toward the end of the 1960s. Things picked up pace when Olle Jonsson, owner of the Pip-Larsson tobacco shop in Malmö, put his pipes in the shop window and persuaded him to use his own stamp; Jonsson's encouragement to visit Sixten Ivarsson established his tie to the Danish School. Nordh continued his work in Malmö. Shapes he developed himself, such as Ramses and Nautilus, have become part of a repertoire repeated in other workshops today.

The second important name is Björn Bengtsson of Malmö. Drawn to the craft by repair jobs that came into his mother's tobacco shop, Bengtsson became an apprentice under Poul Rasmussen in Copenhagen in 1964, at just sixteen. After his master died in 1967 he continued working in the workshop of Rasmussen's widow, Anne Julie; in 1974 he returned to Sweden and began producing under his own name. These pipes, known by the name Björn of Sweden, carry a three- or four-digit number in the stamp marking the month and year of production. When demand fell in the early 1990s, Bengtsson took another job and chose to make pipes part-time; he died in 2023 at seventy-four.
The Present Day

There is no factory-scale pipe production in Sweden today. Production continues in the workshops of a small number of independent makers, most working in the Skåne region; Svenska Pipklubben's publications track these names regularly. Moving between freehand bodies and classic proportions, this production is considered Sweden's branch of the Scandinavian tradition.

r.x: Jeff Gracik

is an American artisan pipe maker who works under the J. Alan name in San Diego, California. The most detailed record of his early years is an interview prepared by Bear Graves for Smokingpipes.com and dated 2007; in it, the maker lays out, in his own words, the names who influenced him, his approach to shape, and his habits at the bench.
Path and Mentors

Reportedly born in 1979, Gracik took up pipe making while a graduate student; sources give varying years for his start, somewhere between 2003 and 2005. His first steps are said to have been self-taught, guided by a widely used pipe-making manual and advice from maker Tim West. He later found the chance to work at the benches of three makers: Jody Davis, Todd Johnson, and the Danish maker Tonni Nielsen. In the interview he counts all three among the defining influences on his work; he states that he learned much of his technique in Johnson's workshop, while the aesthetic approach Nielsen passed on to him in 2005 still shows in his work today. At the time of the interview he was living on the Southern California coast and working there.
Character of the Work and the Bench

Two great traditions stand behind J. Alan's shapes: classic English forms and the line of the Danish School. To these is added a nautical thread that he traces to summers spent sailing on the East Coast, one Gracik describes as the most distinctive vein running through his own work. On the finishing side, J. Alan pipes are given only smooth or sandblasted finishes. Mouthpieces are individually hand-cut from vulcanite, cumberland, or vintage stock bakelite; accent materials such as bamboo, boxwood, and silver are used selectively. Gracik says that in the early years of his career he focused his attention on the internal airway of the briar bowl, and that he developed his natural chamber coating, aimed at shortening the break-in period, only after that phase. Every pipe is stamped with a production serial number and the year it was made; sources give the name of the top grade as "Wave."
Away from the Bench

Gracik himself smokes a pipe; in the interview he states that he prefers full-bodied blends in the style of English blends and Balkan blends. His family, coffee he roasts himself, and music are counted among his main interests away from the bench. Records indicate that in 2015 he founded Alan Brothers with his brother Jeremy, a separate bench-made line working with a more limited range of shapes.

r.x: Robert L. Smith

is the American inventor who, after twenty years of pursuing a single idea, designed a metal-bodied filter pipe and produced it under the Filto name in North Carolina. His name appears in pipe history neither as a carver nor as a factory owner; his real trace lies in the three separate pipe patents he left in the registration record. Because these patents document a single idea maturing step by step, they also serve as a fine example of why pipe patents are useful for dating.
The Patent Chain

Smith's first application is dated 3 April 1946 and was not granted until 17 February 1953, as No. 2,628,622. The document lists the inventor's name as Robert Lequeux Smith and his residence as San Diego. In this first design, the stem is a heat exchanger with fins opening outward: smoke cools as it travels along a helical path, then passes through a chamber packed with fresh tobacco. A second application, filed on 5 January 1949, resulted in a grant on 6 October 1953 as No. 2,654,370; here Smith's address is recorded as Portsmouth. This document describes a bowl-shaped baffle that redirects the smoke, paired with a replaceable, perforated-base filter basket packed with tobacco.

The third and best-known document was filed on 17 October 1963 and granted on 23 February 1965 as No. 3,170,468. This time the applicant had assigned rights to Burgaw-based Filto Pipes, Inc. The patent text explicitly references the two earlier documents and notes that an intervening application had been abandoned. Its innovation is twofold: the filter basket hangs inside the shank on two thin legs, allowing smoke to circulate around the basket's edges so tar cannot collect and block the passage. The flexible cap at the end of the stem snaps on and off like a press-stud. The basket's protruding tabs let the filter be pulled out and discarded without touching it by hand.
Filto Pipes

Filto belongs to the American branch of metal-stemmed devices gathered under pipe filters and systems, and in construction it recalls the pipes of the Kirsten Pipe Company. The stem is a metal cylinder; an absorbent filter fitted inside is held in place by a clip, and smoke circulates around the filter's edges, leaving part of the tar behind. According to collectors who have examined surviving examples, the briar bowl screws onto the shank, the mouthpiece is hard rubber, and bowls and stems were produced in different colours that could be interchanged — though no official manufacturer record confirms these details. On known examples, the shank stamp runs three lines: "FILTO" at the top, "BURGAW, N.C." below it, and a patent and manufacturing-location note at the bottom.

Within the community, the brand is associated with the mid-1960s. Collectors relate that Smith transferred the business to Dr. Grabow in the 1970s and that production ceased shortly afterward; no documentary record currently supports this account. Filto pipes are no longer produced and are now found only in secondary circulation.
