r.x: The search for the first Shell

is the name given to the debate over which year can be assigned to the earliest pipes Dunhill released with a sandblasted finish. Since no dated catalogue page or announcement introducing the series is known, the earliest years must be read from two indirect sources: the timeline of the registration paperwork and the stamps struck on the shanks of the pipes. The oil-curing and sandblasting sequence covered by the patent is discussed in the entry The History of Dunhill Shell Briar.
The Timeline of the Registration Paperwork

rows: American application filed under serial no. 258,053

r.x: The filing date shows that the American application was prepared without waiting for the British document to be issued. It is reported that the Canadian paperwork lagged the American process by a year at both stages, with the application filed in 1919 and the document granted in 1921; neither of these has been confirmed by an independent registration record. For the general place of patent records in dating, see the entry pipe patents.
What the Stamps Can and Cannot Tell Us

Because the year-code system was not settled until the early 1920s (compilations place its start somewhere between 1921 and 1922), the only measure available for Shells made before that is the form of the stamp itself. The most common pattern is DUNHILL'S "SHELL" over MADE IN ENGLAND followed by one of two pairs of lines: PAT. MAR.9.15 with PAT.APP FOR, referencing the American registration, or PAT.1914 with PAT.APP FOR, referencing the Canadian one. Because "application filed" on the second line shows that the sandblasting patent had not yet been finalized in that market, these pipes fall into roughly the 1919-1921 range. The same years also show the stamp 5861/12 . 119708/17, combining the inner-bore and sandblasting patents on a single line. (The inner-bore number is written as 5816/12 in some compilations; the registration record gives 5861/12.)

British stamps follow a rule of their own: unlike American and Canadian stamps, they show the year the application was filed rather than the year the document was granted, which is why the Shell reads 119708/17. Since the number could only be cut into the mold after registration, and allowing time for the mold to be made, a pipe bearing the British Shell patent number is dated no earlier than 1919. A breakdown of the stamp families is given in the entry Dunhill patent stamps and dating.
The Case for a Pre-1918 Date

The view that the series was sold before the British document was issued rests, in collector literature, on a handful of outlier examples examined by John C. Loring. On these pipes, the flat panel where the stamp is struck was carved into the wood rather than leveled flush with the sandblasted surface; this treatment is reportedly not found in production after 1919. One example bears DUNHILL.LONDON over "SHELL BRIAR" and the words U.S.A. PAT / APPLD FOR. The stamp is anomalous in two respects: the brand name lacks the possessive, and it lacks the country-of-origin marking then required for goods shipped to America. The fact that the city line under the brand name changed from DUKE ST. S.W. to LONDON at the end of 1918 is also used as a yardstick for reading these examples.

Building on this, the argument holds that the first Shells went on sale in the autumn of 1917, when the British application was filed, and reached officers at the front before the war ended. The case rests on a single collector source; since no example that can be assigned to before 1918 beyond dispute has yet been produced, the series' first year continues to be argued by inference rather than settled by documentation.

r.x: The Lyon Pipe
is a two-chamber pipe design, its bowls fitting one inside the other, developed by American inventor Charles H. Lyon in Chicago in the early 1920s. Today it is better known as the
Dawes pipe

, so called because it became something close to a personal emblem in the hands of Charles G. Dawes, a well-known figure in American politics. An ordinary workshop invention turning into a national campaign symbol is a story with few parallels in pipe history.
The Logic of the Design

Lyon's solution rests on splitting the bowl in two rather than carving it as a single piece. The inner bowl, where the tobacco burns, screws into the outer chamber. According to the patent text, when the deep threading on the outside of the inner bowl meets the shallow threading inside the outer one, a spiral, winding smoke passage forms between them. Smoke slows in this passage, changes direction, and sheds some of the solid particles it carries; only after this does it reach the shank channel through the opening beneath the inner bowl. The patent text claims this arrangement "purifies" the smoke. Placing a second cavity between the chamber where the tobacco burns and the path to the mouthpiece is an approach we also encounter in the calabash pipe. A removable plug at the bottom of the bowl makes cleaning easier.

That the threading performs both joining and filtering at once — a "double duty" placed on the threads, in the patent's own words — is the design's most original aspect. For another example of the period's search for a smoke channel, see the article on the Falk patent.
The Inventor and a Twist of Fate

Records describe Lyon as a former mill machinist who had lost his right arm in a factory accident during the First World War. By the end of 1920 he was out of work, and nearing sixty, was looking for a new way to make a living. The idea for the pipe was born during that search; the patent application was filed on September 23, 1920, and the registration completed on September 18, 1923.

The story goes that Lyon, noticing that Dawes smoked a pipe, sent him a sample in 1921. Dawes liked the design and began ordering it by the dozen; the two became friends over time. According to one account, based on Lyon's obituary published in early 1947, the two even became partners in production in later years; no other record confirming this partnership has been found.
Becoming a Campaign Symbol

Dawes became Calvin Coolidge's running mate in the 1924 election and handed the pipe out as a campaign gift; the party used it almost as an emblem. After the nomination was announced, the small workshop outside Chicago could no longer keep up with demand. According to a Chicago-datelined report in the Ellensburg Daily Record of September 11, 1924, the backlog of orders had reached 75,000, while production stayed around a thousand pipes a month. These figures rest on a single newspaper report and have not been independently confirmed.

Dawes served as Vice President from 1925 to 1929, shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1925, and later served as Ambassador to the United Kingdom. This visibility gave Lyon's design an extraordinary degree of recognition at a time when the briar pipe was already widespread in America. Today, examples stamped Lyon and Dawes are counted as collector's pieces documenting the mechanical pipe experiments of the early twentieth century.

r.x: "Try this at Home"
is an article credited, according to its byline, to collector Rich Esserman, published in
The Pipe Collector

, the newsletter of the North American Society of Pipe Collectors, and later reprinted with permission on Pipedia. Its subject is tidying up secondhand pipes with everyday household materials instead of sending them to a workshop. The piece's standing in the community comes less from the specific steps it lists than from the attitude it argues for: the author openly admits he has no particular gift for handiwork, and builds his whole approach on that admission.
The Restorer's Bench, the Collector's Table

The fast tools of professional restoration — buffing wheels, sandpaper, heat guns — deliver quick results in an experienced hand and irreversible damage in an inexperienced one. The article's proposed way out is to trade tool speed for slowness: soft abrasives, solvents, and repetition instead of powered machinery. For a restorer this is inefficient, since it takes many times longer to finish the same job. For the amateur, though, it lowers the risk of ruin and leaves the thing that actually matters — the pipe's original character — untouched.
Three Things Worth Protecting

The principle of least intervention takes concrete shape at three points in the text. The first is the line of the stem: held against a buffing wheel too long, a mouthpiece's sharp edge rounds off, its cross-section thins, and its shape is altered beyond recovery. In a collector's eye, a stem that has gone dull but was never touched by a wheel outranks one that gleams but has been thinned. The second is the cake inside the bowl; it is not scraped down to bare wood but left as a thin, slightly rough layer. The third is the stampings on the shank (nomenclature): when working with steam or solvent, the stamped area is masked off, and if there is a flaw there, it is left as it is. This threefold care is the practical expression of the authenticity debate that surrounds the concept of the estate pipe.
What's in the Cupboard, and the Limits of the Job

The materials the article lists come out of the kitchen and bathroom cabinet: silica-bearing toothpaste and baking soda as mild abrasives, high-proof alcohol to dissolve tar, olive oil to bring back faded color, carnauba wax for shine, and orange shellac that dissolves in alcohol. The greenish-brown film that forms on vulcanite stems is the main target of this arsenal; hardened rubber oxidizes at the surface in daylight, and the sulfur it releases combines with moisture to leave a film behind. On sandblasted or rusticated surfaces, where wax won't hold, shellac is used instead, since it is thought not to clog the pores. The ghost smell left by a previous owner is handled less by reaming than by softening and thinning the layer with alcohol and scrubbing the inner surface with baking soda.

The text also draws its own limits: charred wood, a snapped shank, and deep gouges that have cost wood cannot be fixed under home conditions. Because every application of heat, steam, and solvent carries a risk of irreversible damage, leaving the job to a professional is the standard advice for valuable or sentimental pipes. For everyday maintenance and detailed repair, see the entry on pipe repair and mouthpiece care.

r.x: Tobacciana

is the name given to the collecting field devoted to objects produced around tobacco and its consumption. Pipes and tampers, snuff boxes, cigar cutters and bands, tobacco tins, matchboxes, box labels, posters, and promotional print matter form the field's everyday material. Within this broad repertoire researchers also identify one particular thread: objects carrying erotic or explicit imagery, ranging from mere suggestion to outright depiction. The article below summarizes that thread as a historical phenomenon; it does not reproduce images or detailed descriptions of the objects themselves.
Sexual Imagery in Advertising and Print

In the last quarter of the century, tobacco companies made pairing their products with female figures a standard promotional device. In the United States, the picture cards inserted into cigarette packs began in 1879 with Allen & Ginter; the earliest series placed portraits of actresses alongside boxers and baseball players, tribal chiefs, flags, and wild animals. Cigar box labels and wall posters drew on the same repertoire, often with a freer hand. The period's visual art pursued the same connection independently: the Belgian painter and printmaker Félicien Rops (1833-1898) is known for the prints and drawings he made for nineteenth-century erotic literature, and his name comes up often in studies of the smoking woman as a period icon.
The Image Inside the Lens

The miniature photograph hidden inside a keepsake object grew out of the technical curiosity of the mid-nineteenth century. In 1857 René Dagron found a way to fix a microphotograph to the tip of a slender cylindrical lens; in this device — named for the Stanhope lens whose form he adapted — the image appears magnified when the lens is held up to a light source. The pieces Dagron called "photographic-microscopic jewels" were set into rings, ivory trinkets, pens, sewing implements, even violin bows. Collecting literature also counts pipes with a lens set into the mouthpiece or stem among the same family; according to that same literature, some of the images chosen were erotic scenes rather than the usual churches, monuments, and city views. What set the device apart was that the image was visible only to whoever raised the lens to their eye — not to anyone simply looking at the object.
In Mold, Porcelain, and Stone

Molding and carving left pipe makers a wide range of subject matter. Nineteenth-century molded clay pipes were produced in an enormous variety of forms, including portraits, animal figures, topical political caricatures, and outright explicit scenes; the literature on clay pipe archaeology reports that examples falling into this last group were seized and destroyed by customs authorities. Colored transfer printing, which became common on German porcelain pipe bowls in the second half of the nineteenth century, offered a far cheaper way to reproduce imagery than hand painting and broadened the range of subjects treated. Meerschaum, for its part, became the leading material for figural carving thanks to how readily it could be worked; the figural pipe tradition that continued in European workshops and later in Eskişehir meerschaum carving showed a range running from classical busts to erotic subjects.
Collections and the Boundary Question

The assembling of such objects has occasionally entered the record for political reasons. Genrikh Yagoda, who headed the Soviet secret police, the NKVD, from 1934 to 1936, was arrested in March 1937, and both his two residences in Moscow and his dacha were searched; according to the account based on the search record, 3,904 pornographic photographs, 11 films, and 165 obscenely carved pipes and cigarette holders were logged. Corruption was also among the charges against Yagoda; he was tried and shot in March 1938.
Reading the pipe as a sexual image is not solely a matter for collectors: in
The Interpretation of Dreams

, Sigmund Freud proposed a reading of the pipe as the formal counterpart of the male sexual organ, and that reading is frequently cited in the field's literature. Whether such objects should be counted as art or as explicit material remains an unresolved debate in collecting circles today; the criterion rarely goes beyond the collector's own judgment. A similar impasse has entered the legal record as well: in the U.S. Supreme Court's 1964 ruling in Jacobellis v. Ohio, Justice Potter Stewart openly declined to define obscenity, settling instead for saying he would know it when he saw it. For the broader framework of how the pipe moved from a utilitarian object to one of display and collection, see the World History of the Pipe article.

r.x: Handmade or machine-made?

The distinction reads as a clean opposition in catalog and stamp language, but where briar pipes are concerned, neither extreme actually holds in practice. It is not possible to finish a pipe from start to finish with hand tools alone, nor to have one come off a lathe untouched by human hands. The trade has coined a third category for the broad space in between:
hand made by machine
The Limit Set by Briar

Clay and meerschaum are soft while being worked; both can be carved deeply with a knife, and a mistaken cut can be corrected. Briar, by contrast, is hard, and prone to chipping and cracking. The outside of the bowl can be shaped with a file and sandpaper, and the tobacco chamber can be hollowed by hand; the trouble comes with two holes. Neither the smoke channel running from the shank end to the chamber floor, nor the airway running through the mouthpiece, can be drilled by hand with sufficient accuracy or without risking the material. For this reason, no briar pipe today can truly be called entirely handmade. Where these holes sit within the body is shown in the pipe anatomy article.
What the Machine Leaves Undone

The limit runs the other way too. A duplicating router, following a hand-prepared master, can turn out dozens of bodies from the same pattern in one pass; mouthpieces, too, can be produced by molding. Even so, the piece coming off the machine is not considered finished. The excess left in areas the router cannot reach — called
ears

in workshop language, as it is reported — is sanded away by hand. The mortise that receives the mouthpiece is also opened separately, the mouthpiece is hand-fitted to the shank, mold marks are removed by hand, and staining, polishing, and final inspection are likewise left to human hands. For this reason it is equally hard to speak of a wholly machine-made pipe.
The Methods in Between

Between these two extremes lie a number of quite different working methods. In hand turning, the block is shaped with a chisel while spinning on a lathe; the machine only rotates it, while the hand does the shaping. Sixten Ivarsson is reported to have followed this method until around 1957, after which — because the method by its nature forced round, symmetrical bodies — he switched to free-form shaping on a rotating sanding disc. Makers who built their own rigs form a separate rung: Erik Nørding, known for his engineering background, roughed out the outline of his free-form bodies on a duplicating router at his Nørding workshop and then finished each body individually on the disc. In a third arrangement, the body is bought ready-made from another manufacturer and reshaped by hand; it can go in as one shape and come out as another.
How Binding Is the Term

There is no formal standard separating these stages. The classification most often cited in pipe writing rests on R. D. Field's piece in the Fall 2003 issue of Pipes and Tobaccos: a pipe made using hand tools only counts as handmade, one involving no hand labor at all counts as machine-made, and any mixture of the two counts as hand made by machine. Once the standard is drawn this sharply, the first two categories turn out to be essentially empty in practice.

Looking at another field for comparison is instructive. The federal guidance governing the U.S. jewelry trade requires that, for a product to be marketed as "handmade," every shaping, finishing, and decorating step, starting from the raw material, be done by hand labor and hand-controlled methods, with the maker able to alter the structure and form of each individual piece. No such regulation exists in pipe making; the wording on the stamp is the maker's own claim. And the classification describes a method, not a level of craftsmanship. The relationship between these methods and scale of production is covered in the artisan pipe and factory pipe article.

r.x: Dunhill's long-shank Canadian pipes

appear in the brand's old shape chart under the letters ES, and in the postwar ODA line under the numbers 850 and 851. All three pair a slender, oval-sectioned, elongated shank with a mid-sized bowl, and at a glance they are difficult to tell apart. What sets this trio apart in the collecting literature, though, is not their resemblance to one another but the fact that each of the three codes has a rare variant with a shank far longer than its usual measurement.
What Distinguishes The Three Codes

On a standard ES, the shank runs roughly seven and a half centimeters from the back of the bowl to where the mouthpiece begins, and the mouthpiece itself has a flattened oval section. On the 850 and 851, by contrast, the shank starts thicker at the bowl and tapers toward the mouthpiece, and both have a tapered oval mouthpiece. The 851's mouthpiece is noticeably long, which lengthens the pipe overall: a 1963 Shell 851 measures over 19 centimeters, while a 1964 Root Briar 850 comes in at roughly 16.6 centimeters. The 851 is rare in any finish. The 845, the series' third Canadian, is the most commonly encountered Canadian in the ODA line and is genuinely large-bowled; its shank typically runs between seven and eight and a half centimeters, and a 1973 Shell example exceeds 17 centimeters overall. Within the Canadian family, ES's smaller-scale counterpart was produced under the EC code; a 1964 Shell EC has been measured at between fourteen and fifteen centimeters.
The Four-Inch Shank

In nearly every year the ES was produced, a handful of examples have turned up with shanks measuring between 10 and 11.5 centimeters; the longest documented shank runs to roughly 11.3 centimeters. Most known pieces date to the 1950s and 1960s. So this is not a shape variation applied in a given year and then dropped, but a measurement that recurred intermittently over half a century. The same rare long shanks turn up on the 850 and 851 as well; no such example is known for the 845, whose longest recorded shank runs to about nine and a half centimeters. A long-shank Canadian demands a briar block larger and more flawless than usual — a single crack or sand pit anywhere along the shank's length ruins the entire piece. How the long shank could exist under the same shape code without ever entering the standard line is not explained by factory records; the question has been debated among collectors ever since John C. Loring compiled the known examples in 2001.
The Codes' Lifespan

The brand has made Canadians since the 1910s; although the ES's bowl grew somewhat larger in the 1920s, the pipe's overall look remained largely stable for half a century. Dunhill's lettered and short-numbered codes, used until the mid-1970s, were organized so that each corresponded to a single shape; even whether the mouthpiece was tapered or saddle-cut required its own code. The meaning of ES is not known with certainty, though the common reading is "extended shank." The ODA series, which records indicate was introduced in 1950 with three-digit numbers starting with 8, comprised shapes noticeably larger than the brand's standard sizes; for details of the series, see the Early Dunhill OD Pipes entry. Of the three Canadians in the series, the 850 is one of the few ODAs pictured in the brand's 1968 wholesale/export catalogue. With the shift to the five-digit system around 1975 — which combined length, mouthpiece type, and bowl shape into a single code — the ES fell out of use, and the 850 and 851 shapes largely disappeared as well.

r.x: Peterson System Standard

is the most common and plainest version of "System," the best-known design of the Dublin firm Kapp & Peterson. The brand owes much of its worldwide reputation to this mechanism: a reservoir meant to catch the moisture in the smoke before it reaches the smoker, paired with a specially shaped mouthpiece that directs the smoke toward the palate. In Peterson's catalogue, System pipes still stand as a separate family.
The Sequence of Patents

The system's present form is not the result of a single invention but of several patents that build on one another. According to records, the first patent dates to 1890 and covers the moisture reservoir carved into the transition area between shank and bowl; the reservoir is created by raising the smoke channel higher than usual, leaving an empty space beneath it. The stepped mouthpiece bore is cited to 1891, and the mouthpiece tip known as P-Lip to patents from 1894 and 1898. Added to these was the army mount, the metal band wrapping around the shank, and the mechanism arrived at its present-day identity.
How the Mechanism Works

Smoke leaving the bowl does not go straight from the shank's channel to the mouthpiece; it first descends into the reservoir. What makes this happen is the extension at the end of the mouthpiece that fits into the pipe: it passes through the transition bore and hangs down into the reservoir, circulating the smoke at the bottom. Part of the condensing moisture is thus caught in the reservoir before it ever reaches the mouthpiece. On plain models such as the System Standard, this extension is turned from a single piece of vulcanite together with the mouthpiece; on upper-tier System pipes it is a separate metal part screwed into the mouthpiece. On older examples it is brass, on later ones aluminium. Because its appearance resembles the condensation needles of other brands, it is often removed by mistake; in fact the extension is the working part of the mechanism, and removing it disables the reservoir.

The mouthpiece's internal bore is also not a constant width from end to end; it changes in steps. It is known that after a narrow section at the entrance, the channel widens, then narrows again as it nears the tip. It is accepted that smoke slowing down in the widened section sheds its moisture more easily. At the tip of the P-Lip, the hole is not centred but sits on the upper face; this directs the smoke toward the palate rather than onto the tongue. The aim is to reduce tongue bite.
Use and Debate

The P-Lip is one of the few details that divide opinion within the pipe community. Some smokers praise the grip it gives when held between the teeth; others complain that hot smoke concentrates at a single point on the palate. Cleaning is a similarly contested topic. A pipe cleaner is expected to go in one end and come out the other without catching; on small-scale, sharply curved System examples this is not always possible. In practice, working with thin cleaners and wiping the reservoir separately by removing the mouthpiece is considered sufficient. For details, see the pipe cleaning and maintenance entry.

The System Standard series is made from good-quality briar, and offered with a nickel mount and an army-type push mouthpiece. The series is known for smooth and rustic finishes together with tones ranging from dark walnut to red and ebony black. Nearly all the shapes are bent (curved), and the catalogue contains a single straight model. For the brand's design experiments outside of System, see the Peterson Darwin series and the B42 shape entry.

r.x: Amy Lawrence Lowell

(1874-1925) is one of the most discussed names in early 20th-century American poetry, and an unusual figure in tobacco history. Born into Boston's storied Lowell family, the poet did not hide her cigar in an era when women smoking in the open was considered improper; the meerschaum pipes attributed to her in collections have carried her name into pipe literature as well.
Life and Poetry

She was born on 9 February 1874 in Brookline, Massachusetts, at the family's Sevenels estate, where she spent most of her life. She never attended university, educating herself instead in her father's library and among the shelves of the Boston Athenæum. Among her brothers, Percival Lowell was an astronomer and Abbott Lawrence Lowell served as president of Harvard University. She came to writing late: her first collection,
A Dome of Many-Coloured Glass

, appeared in 1912. She soon became the American spokesperson for the Imagist movement, compiling three Imagist anthologies; once the movement's direction had taken shape under her hand, Ezra Pound dismissively called it "Amygism." She died of a cerebral hemorrhage at Sevenels on 12 May 1925, and the following year was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry for
What's O'Clock
. Her rare-book and manuscript collection was donated to Harvard University, and is preserved today in a room bearing her name at the Houghton Library.
Her Cigar Habit and Public Image

Lowell's cigar smoking was a fixture the press of her time never tired of. Newspapers presented her as a woman puffing large, dark cigars. According to reports, what she actually smoked was quite different: thin, mild Manila cigars from the Philippines and small panatelas. In Barbara L. Bellows's 2006 study
A Talent for Living

, it is noted that when Sevenels was renovated, she had a humidity-controlled storage room built dedicated solely to her cigars. Being mocked for her size, her masculine-cut clothing, and her habits did not deter her from this visibility; the nickname "hippopoetess," coined by a rival poet, is a trace of that reaction. Her name is often mentioned today in collections of famous pipe and tobacco smokers, in listings of women smokers.
The Pipe: Objects and Conflicting Accounts

The most concrete trace of her relationship to the pipe survives in objects. A meerschaum pipe exhibited in the George Arents tobacco collection at the New York Public Library is attributed to her; an article introducing the collection puts the number of pipes said to have come from the poet at as many as forty. The same account also notes that Lowell's only known habit was cigars, recording the contradiction in its own text. Reports say a meerschaum pipe attributed to the poet was also displayed at a 1983 exhibition of literary memorabilia at the Grolier Club in New York, and that the club held seven of her unsmoked Filipino cigars.

Written testimony, however, doesn't agree. Horace Gregory's 1958 biography reports that she occasionally smoked a pipe behind closed doors — after breakfast at her country house, or in bed at Sevenels. Bellows, on the other hand, writes that the pipe was too much trouble for her. In the October 1948 issue of
Pipe Lovers

magazine, drawing on the manager of D. P. Ehrlich, a Boston tobacconist, it's reported that Lowell chose the lightest pipes she could find and insisted on the thinnest possible mouthpiece. In her known poems, the word "pipe" appears in only two lengthy works, "The Cremona Violin" and "The Great Adventure of Max Breuck"; in both, the pipe is a prop that sets the scene. Though it's a familiar image to writings that trace meerschaum's footprint in literature, these lines are not proof of the poet's own habit. Unlike writers like J. B. Priestley, who became identified with their pipe, Lowell passes into tobacco history not with a portrait of a habitual smoker, but with a collecting question the sources have never resolved.

r.x: Ashton

is a brand founded in England in 1983 that made a name for itself among top-tier briar pipemakers within just a few years. Its origin lies in the meeting of two people: William John Taylor, a maker trained at the Alfred Dunhill factory, and R. D. Field, the importer who took on the brand's distribution in the United States. Field's first-hand account of the founding years, titled "The Ashton Pipe Story," is the primary source for details from this early period.
From the Dunhill Bench to His Own Brand

According to accounts, Taylor joined Alfred Dunhill as a lathe operator in 1959, at fifteen. The apprenticeship at the factory was a long one: newcomers spent years on support tasks before reaching the bench, and most experienced pipemakers kept their own methods to themselves. Taylor built up this knowledge over time and decided to found his own brand in the early 1980s. The name Ashton was settled in talks with Field early in 1983; known records put the number of pipes that left the workshop that year at thirty-one. Taylor left his job in 1984 to move fully into his own workshop, and as a mark of confidence in the brand, added Ashton to his surname, taking the name William John Ashton-Taylor.
Production Method

Two processes define Ashton's technical identity. The first is oil curing. According to the maker's own description, turned bowls are first heated for eight hours, then soaked for eight hours in a mixture of three different oils, then mounted on heated brass pins and left for fourteen days. Over this time, the oil seeping back out of the wood carries with it the sap and residue remaining in the briar.

The second is deep sandblasting. The brand's dark PebbleGrain finish, with its large, deep texture, is often compared to early Dunhill Shell pipes; this look is considered a major reason the brand became recognizable so quickly. Taylor later developed an intermediate process he called PebbleShell: once curing is finished, the bowl is steamed to raise the soft grain, the raised grain is carved away, and only then is the piece sandblasted. This yields a more gnarled surface. Reports say this method was granted an English patent, with the patent number stamped on the pipes. Other finishes include the naturally sandblasted Old Church and the smooth-finished Sovereign, Oak, Claret, and Brindle.

There is a distinctive approach on the mouthpiece side, too. Vulcanite rod is boiled for an extended period before being shaped into a mouthpiece, to strip out as much sulfur as possible; this is said to delay oxidation. In the early 1990s, a material called Ashtonite, sitting between vulcanite and acrylic, came into use.
Sizes, Stamps, and Succession

The brand became known in the American market for its large-bowled pipes. Size stamps run from small to large as X, XX, XXX, LX, and ELX; above these sits the very limited Magnum series. The ELX appeared in 1984 and the Magnum in 1985. Dating relies on the number following the "Made in England" mark: it starts at 3 for 1983 and increases by one each year, a practice that continued into the mid-2000s. The first year's pipes were stamped simply with the letters and "Made in London England," without a finish name.

The workshop never employed more than two full-time people at any point; part-time hands were occasionally brought on for support tasks. In this respect the brand sits at the boundary between artisan production and factory organization. William Ashton-Taylor passed away on 16 September 2009. Production continues under Jimmy Craig, who worked alongside him in his later years; pipes made by Craig usually carry a "JC" mark alongside the standard stamps.

r.x: Brad Pohlmann

is an American pipemaker who entered the craft in the mid-1970s, worked in an entirely different trade for more than twenty years in between, and then returned to the bench. His name is associated both with the second generation of the American handmade pipe scene and with the small number of makers who build most of their own tools.
The Vermont Years

His interest in pipes began in high school, at a tobacco shop in Alhambra, California. After a trip taken to see Britain's storied pipe houses in person, he began looking for a master to teach him the craft; when his search in New York turned up nothing, he joined The Briar Workshop, run by Elliott Nachwalter and Jorg Jemelka in Stowe, Vermont, in the fall of 1976. He worked unpaid the first few weeks, gradually became involved in every stage of production, and developed particular expertise in staining and final finishing. The same crew included J. T. Cooke, who would later become known under his own name. Pohlmann stayed at the workshop for about five years; the venture dissolved after it relocated to Florida.
The Long Gap Between

During this period, Pohlmann decided that becoming a lasting pipemaker meant mastering machining. He completed a four-year, eight-thousand-hour tool-and-die apprenticeship. A long corporate career followed: he spent roughly sixteen years at Tandem Computers, leaving when the company passed first to Compaq and then to Hewlett-Packard. By his own account, these years also gave him the chance to work with the owner of the now-closed Arlington pipe factory, and with makers who had worked there, such as Charlie Tusa.

Most sources give his return to the bench as 2003; some accounts place it a year later. Through his former workshop colleague Cooke, he acquired a stock of briar that had been resting for fifteen years. Working a few times at Todd Johnson's workshop, whom he met at the Chicago pipe show, proved a turning point; there he learned the "shape first, drill after" method. In this sequence, where the holes are bored only after the block has been shaped, the grain direction can be followed more closely to produce freer forms.
Workmanship and Signature Features

In Pohlmann's pipes, the mouthpiece is cut by hand from rod stock rather than a pre-made mold, and seats onto the body with a Delrin tenon; along with vulcanite, he also works with bakelite. His shape language leaned initially toward the Danish school; the maker has said that in later years he moved toward sharper lines and a more flowing direction. Among the influences he has named in interviews are S. Bang, Tom Eltang, Kei'ichi Gotoh, Yuki Tokutomi, Cornelius Mänz, and Paolo Becker. For accent pieces he uses tamarind wood, boxwood, blackwood palm, horn, and bamboo; on the surface, he moves between a polished finish and sandblasts of his own devising. The pipes carry a script "Pohlmann" stamp with "USA" beneath it.

The maker works today in Oregon's Applegate valley, in a workshop he shares with his wife and fellow maker Silver Gray. His building most of his own lathes and jigs is often cited as the main reason for the precision frequently noted in his work.
